chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Territory bands: Speed Webb, Zach White and Frank Terry's Chicago Nightingales
summary: Hinton cites Elgar's records and a book of territory bands; Wilson recalls Ohio bands and the hundreds of dance bands working through the Depression.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Well, Teddy, we'll just get back onto you, then. We were talking about Charlie Elgar, which was one of the band leaders, a violinist. And I think he was probably one of our greatest black historians because Charlie kept records of everything, all the teachers of the big bands and all the bands of that era. And I remember this book that I think I mentioned to you once before, a guy named McCarthy in England, has written a book about jazz. And he's got the most extensive one that I've seen on the territory bands, Alfonso Trent. He's got pictures of all these bands. And I don't know where in the world he could have gotten them. I don't know too many people (inaudible) Kansas State, somewhere.

Somewhere I've got a picture of that Speed Webb band, which was operating the same time as Trent. Zach White's band, I've seen pictures of that group. And Frank Terry, the Chicago Nightingales, do you remember that group?
Oh, that's one on me, Teddy.
You never heard of that group?

They were an Ohio band, they were very popular around Ohio. They were like Zach and Speed. Frank Terry and his Chicago Nightingales. And oh, they kept busy on the road. And (inaudible). Buffalo to Cleveland. But

people were dancing to that kind of music in those days so there were just hundreds and hundreds of those bands, all working, not making much money because the Depression was on. But everybody was working. People were dancing. Save up a few dollars to go out. Dance halls, open air in the summer in towns, closed in in winters. All amusement parks had dancing.
